clue.text: Vacillating oily brat, neutral at heart?

definitions.text: Vacillating oily brat, neutral at heart?

indicators.note: at heart means the next piece is placed in the middle of the shuffled letters
something vacillating sways back and forth, so the letters of the two words that follow are shaken into a new order

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for neutral, as on an electrical plug or a gear lever

explanation.surface: A sneer at a slippery, spoilt young politician who claims to sit in the middle of the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the wordplay builds the name, and the clue as a whole is the setter's jibe at the new Labour leader as a wavering centrist.
explanation.definitionFit: Blair took the Labour leadership in 1994 and moved the party to the centre, which the setter mocks as fence-sitting.

clue.text: Piss while holding pint get it everywhere

indicators.note: while holding means the first word wraps round the next piece

parts.note: slash is British slang for an act of urinating
P is a standard abbreviation for pint

explanation.surface: A crude picture of a drunk relieving himself, beer in hand, and making a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a slash' is British slang for urinating.
explanation.definitionFit: To splash is to scatter liquid so that it goes all over the place.

clue.text: Rich and famous lush resort

parts.note: a lush is a heavy drinker; the place celebrities go to dry out is a well-known American rehab centre

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush resort' reads like a luxurious holiday spot, but a lush is a drunkard, and the resort is where the wealthy go to be treated for addiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Californian rehab centre, founded by a former First Lady, is famous for treating celebrities for alcohol and drug addiction.

clue.text: Balls-up of continental cable broadcast

parts.note: de is the French for of, so a continental of

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered widely, so the letters of the word cable are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: A complaint about a cock-up in a European cable television transmission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like part of the television picture with 'cable', but it is the signal to rearrange CABLE into BACLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A balls-up is British slang for a complete mess or fiasco, which is what a debacle is.

clue.text: Your place or mine?

parts.note: the chat-up line is read literally as asking whose dwelling to go to

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the classic pick-up line; read flatly, 'place' just means home.
explanation.definitionFit: An abode is a home or dwelling, the 'place' in the line, whether yours or mine.

clue.text: Miss western-style row with one old foe of Thatcher

parts.note: gal is the American, cowboy-film word for a girl or miss
a tier is a row, as of seats
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A girl in a Wild West row with a single old enemy of the Iron Lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Leopoldo Galtieri led the Argentine junta that invaded the Falklands in 1982.
explanation.definitionFit: As Argentina's ruler during the Falklands War he was Thatcher's military opponent.

clue.text: A dick's an interesting and amusing organ!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dick is slang for a detective, a private investigator
second meaning: the satirical magazine in which this crossword appears, an organ being a periodical

explanation.walkthrough: Both 'dick' and 'organ' tempt a smutty reading; one is a detective, the other a publication, and the setter is plugging his own magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is American slang for a hired detective and also the title of the British satirical fortnightly.

clue.text: Toolbox kid wants scrap

parts.note: to cod is dated British slang for to hoax or kid someone
a scrap is a piece, a small fragment

explanation.surface: A child who wants scraps of wood or metal from a toolbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toolbox' looks like a box of spanners, but the tool is the man's own, and the box is the pouch that held it in Tudor breeches.
explanation.definitionFit: A codpiece was a pouch covering the genitals on men's breeches, jokingly a box for a 'tool', slang for penis.

clue.text: See 1
Heartless Tory bluster from a leader like Thatcher?

indicators.note: heartless means the word Tory loses its middle letters, leaving only its ends

parts.note: to rant is to bluster, to talk loudly and angrily

explanation.surface: A sneer at a callous Conservative ranting like the Iron Lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyrant is a cruel, domineering ruler, which is what her critics called Thatcher; the question mark flags the opinion.

clue.text: Monosodium glutamate, for example, is like coke decarbonised

indicators.note: decarbonised means the carbon, chemical symbol C, is taken out

parts.note: coke here is cocaine, which is addictive

explanation.surface: A food scientist comparing a flavour enhancer to a fizzy drink or to fuel with the carbon removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coke' suggests the drink or the fuel, either of which might be decarbonised; it is the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Monosodium glutamate is a flavour enhancer put into processed food, an example of an additive.

clue.text: See 18
Intimate peep amongst our smalls?

parts.note: smalls are the small ads, and an intimate peep is a meeting of glances, the name of the magazine's lonely-hearts listing

explanation.walkthrough: Smalls is British slang for underwear, so the clue looks like knicker-sniffing; here smalls are small ads, where readers seek romance under this heading.
explanation.definitionFit: Meeting someone's gaze is an intimate look, and the phrase doubles as a pun on the magazine's name for its personal ads.

clue.text: This MP needs maybe a double one inside to get hard on

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means added after what comes before
inside means the numeral is put within the wager word

parts.note: a double is a kind of bet, staking on two races
I is the Roman numeral one
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A politician who needs a double measure inside him to get an erection.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Beith was the Liberal Democrat MP for Berwick-upon-Tweed and his party's deputy leader.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a particular Member of Parliament, and 'this MP' asks for his surname.

clue.text: Rave over cat who put squeeze on members

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above, so this comes first

parts.note: a rave is a party
the cat-o'-nine-tails is a whip

explanation.surface: A cat getting excited, then someone squeezing body parts.
explanation.walkthrough: In Parliament a whip is the officer who enforces party discipline, making members vote the party line.
explanation.definitionFit: A party whip pressures the party's MPs, its members, to turn up and vote as instructed.

clue.text: Stops you from playing bloody joker

parts.note: blood is red
a card is a joker, a comic person

explanation.surface: Someone's swearing at a practical joker who keeps spoiling the game.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a red card sends a player off, so it bars him from playing on.

clue.text: Rocker mounts lover Norma no longer

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounts means sits on top of what follows

parts.note: a rocker is a rocking chair
a woman's man is her lover

explanation.surface: A rocker climbing on top of the Prime Minister's wife, her husband no longer.
explanation.walkthrough: Read Norma as Norman less its last letter: Sir Norman Fowler had just stepped down as Conservative Party chairman in 1994. The surface hints at Norma Major.
explanation.definitionFit: Fowler held the post of party chairman until 1994, so 'Norma(n) no longer' is a former holder of this office.

clue.text: Can it be possibly about to get limp? That makes a change for some ministers!

definitions.text: That makes a change for some ministers!

indicators.note: possibly means the three words are only one possible order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: re means about, concerning
to shuffle is to walk with a dragging limp

explanation.surface: Is it possible to go limp? Meanwhile, a jibe that ministers are getting a change of scene.
explanation.definitionFit: When a Prime Minister reshuffles the Cabinet, some ministers are moved to new jobs or sacked.

clue.text: Policeman with a hunch — a rotten one

parts.note: a person with a hunched back is bent
cop is slang for a policeman

explanation.surface: A police officer acting on a hunch who turns out to be corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunch' suggests a detective's gut feeling, but it is the hunched back; bent is also slang for corrupt.
explanation.definitionFit: The 'one' is the policeman, and a rotten officer, taking bribes, is called bent.

clue.text: Norma done over by city type

indicators.note: done over means beaten up, so the letters of Norma are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Norma Major beaten up by a City financier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City type' suggests a London banker; the city is Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman is a native of the city of Rome, a type of city dweller.

clue.text: Try to get deceptive slice on balls

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means attached after what precedes it

parts.note: to test something is to try it

indicators.note: a deceptive version is a false arrangement, so the letters of slice are jumbled

explanation.surface: Golf or tennis advice: try to put deceptive slice on the balls.
explanation.walkthrough: The sporting reading makes 'balls' look like the ones being hit; they are the definition, in the slang sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Balls is common slang for the male reproductive glands.

clue.text: See 3
Neuter: maybe Yoko's sex

parts.note: n. is the grammar abbreviation for neuter

indicators.note: maybe shows that the letters of Yoko are only one possible arrangement, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: Speculation on Yoko Ono's gender, or whether hers is neutered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex' looks like gender in the surface; it is the act, for which nooky is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Nooky is playful slang for sexual intercourse.

clue.text: Rumpus not out of place in parliament

parts.note: a storm is an uproar or rumpus

indicators.note: out of place means the letters of the word not are put in a different order

explanation.surface: An uproar in the Commons that was not out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not out' looks like a cricket phrase or the opposite of 'in'; it splits, NOT being the fodder for 'out of place'. Stormont is home of the Northern Ireland parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormont, outside Belfast, houses the Northern Ireland legislature, and the name stands for that parliament.

clue.text: Flow-interrupter attached to party nutter!

indicators.note: attached to means joined on to the next piece

parts.note: a weir is a low dam across a river, interrupting its flow
a do is British slang for a party

explanation.surface: Someone who fits a valve to a party member, a lunatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutter is British slang for a crazy person, and a weirdo is an odd or eccentric one.

clue.text: Squidgy and foreign — but fast

parts.note: Squidgy was the pet name for Princess Diana, Di, on the leaked Squidgygate tapes
ET, the extraterrestrial, is as foreign as it gets

explanation.surface: A soft, foreign sweet that has to be eaten quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: Squidgy suggests a soft texture; it was a caller's nickname for Diana on tapes leaked in 1992.
explanation.definitionFit: To fast is to go without food, and a diet is a restricted eating regime.

clue.text: Lowly official, we hear, but a passionate family man

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by its sound, and in British speech clerk rhymes with lark

parts.note: a clerk is a junior office worker

explanation.surface: A minor functionary who is nonetheless a devoted husband and father.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Clark was a Tory minister notorious for his diaries and his affairs, so 'passionate family man' is ironic.
explanation.definitionFit: The diarist was married with sons, yet his passions famously strayed outside the family.

clue.text: The ins and outs of our daily existence?

definitions.text: The ins and outs of our daily existence?

parts.words: The ins and outs of our daily existence?
parts.note: the idiom for details is read literally as the body's openings through which things go in and out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ins and outs' usually means the details of something; taken literally, it is the openings food and waste pass through.
explanation.definitionFit: Orifices are the body's openings, such as mouth and anus, through which things enter and leave every day.
